## What was wrong

I measured the live deployment and the recent CI runs before touching anything.

**Reads were already fine.** Against `cachet.nox.so` from Vancouver: narinfo 39 ms warm / 133 ms cold, NAR at 38-42 MB/s. cache.nixos.org measures 133 ms and 50 MB/s from the same laptop. The edge cache worked, 404s cached, and curl sends Basic preemptively so the missing `WWW-Authenticate` cost no round trip.

**Reads felt slow because the cache was empty.** Of 300 random local store paths, cachet held 12 (4%); cache.nixos.org held 71. cachet is priority 30, so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and goes upstream anyway.

**The cache was empty because writes were catastrophic.** From CI run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** (974 paths) |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** (830 paths) |

1.34 seconds per object. The push step was forty times the job it exists to accelerate, and pushes that slow do not finish.

## The three costs

**The worker read every NAR back to verify it.** `put_narinfo` did `head()`, then a full `bucket.get()` of the object the client uploaded minutes earlier, then a SHA-256 over the compressed bytes, a ruzstd decode, and a second SHA-256 over every decompressed byte. For rustc: 132 MB re-read, 409 MB decoded, 541 MB hashed, in wasm, per path, three times over on a client retry.

The bytes are now measured by the write that stores them, streaming through the same hashers on their way into the bucket, and the result lands beside the object as a facts document. The narinfo request reads a few hundred bytes instead of a few hundred megabytes. Verify-then-sign is unchanged — `VerifiedNar::verify` takes the same four measured values and the signer still accepts nothing else (ADR 0012). Multipart measures on completion, because its parts arrive out of order; that is the one read-back left, and only objects past 90 MiB reach it.

**The client compressed closures it then threw away.** `nix copy --to file://` staged each survivor's whole closure into a tempdir, so members the cache already held were serialized and compressed at full cost and filtered out afterwards. Each path is now serialized and compressed on its own: `nix store dump-path` streamed through a zstd encoder, hashed as it passes, held in memory below 8 MiB and spilled to one scratch file above. The narinfo is built from `nix path-info --json` rather than copied out of a staging tree.

**Uploads were barriered waves with multipart outside them.** `pipeline.rs:412` was a plain sequential `for` loop over every multipart object, so the fat NARs serialized against each other, and `wave_run` used `join_all` so each wave cost its slowest member. One sliding window now covers everything, parts go eight wide inside it, bodies are an `Arc<[u8]>` or a file range instead of a `Vec` cloned per attempt, and HTTP/2 is on.

## Also fixed

- **The daily GC wiped the global edge cache.** The generation prefixed every cache key and the collector bumps it whenever a sweep deletes anything, so the 30-day `immutable` lifetime could never be reached. A stored object's key no longer carries it; only a cached absence does (ADR 0013).
- **Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** `with_signature` appended unconditionally and `nix copy` preserved existing Sig lines, so every push→substitute→re-push cycle added another. The live cache has narinfos carrying two today; it would have grown until the 64 KiB cap started failing pushes.
- **Worker settings.** `observability`, `placement: smart`, and `cpu_ms: 300_000` were all unset. Without the first, nothing about a slow read was diagnosable from production.
- **Build.** No `[profile.release]` and no RUSTFLAGS, so the wasm shipped without LTO or SIMD. Now 116 KB smaller with 6,259 vector instructions.
- Exponential backoff over five attempts instead of linear over three, and `WWW-Authenticate` on 401s.

## Breaking

A NAR write declares its decompressed size in `x-cachet-nar-bytes`, because the decoder needs a ceiling before the narinfo carrying `NarSize` arrives. Older clients answer 411. The bound is paired with a ratio cap on how far uploaded bytes may expand, so the decompression-amp defense is tighter than it was rather than looser.

## Dependency

The C zstd library enters `cachet-push` through a named wrapper in `deny.toml`, the same shape as the existing `ring` exception: ruzstd decodes and cannot encode, and the client has to produce the NAR it uploads. `cachet-push` and `cachet-cli` compile only for hosts. `check-wasm-hygiene.sh` now scans the artifact for `zstd_sys`/`ZSTD_` too, so the ban protects the bundle rather than the intention — verified green against the built bundle.

## Verification

Every local lane green: `unit` (185 tests), `property`, `golden`, `kani`, `workerd`, `deny`, `wasm-hygiene`, `clippy`, `clippy-wasm`, `openapi-check`, `doc-manifest`, `lane-manifest`, `scripts`, `fmt`.

The workerd lane gained assertions for the new contract: a NAR write without its declared size is 411, bytes that do not hash to the key naming them are refused and deleted, the facts document is unreachable from a request, re-pushing a signed narinfo leaves the signature list unchanged, and a stored object still answers from the edge under a corrupt generation while an absence does not. Its CLI scenario drives the real streaming client end to end, including a 100 MiB multipart payload.

What this does not prove is the deployment. `just destroy` and `just deploy` on a clean bucket, then `just integration`, and compare the post-step push against the 5 m 18 s baseline from run 32806212498 and the 31-minute `openapi` baseline from 32803263823.

## Not done

`cache_verdict` still awaits its KV write on the request path (`verdict.rs:326`), and the per-org membership loop is still sequential. Both are cold-isolate-only, and threading a `Context` through six call sites was a wider change than the rare path justifies.

I also tried holding the probe's bucket enumeration at the edge for a minute. It made things worse and is not in this PR: the memo drifts in the safe direction, but what it drifts away from is exactly the dedup that makes a warm push cheap, and the workerd lane caught a sibling push re-uploading paths it already had.
MD

Here's what I found and did while CI runs.

**Your instinct was half right.** Uploads are exactly as bad as you said. Downloads are not — I measured them.

| | cachet | cache.nixos.org |
| --- | --- | --- |
| narinfo warm / cold | 39 ms / 133 ms | — / 133 ms |
| NAR throughput | 38–42 MB/s | 50 MB/s |

Reads are at parity. They *feel* slow because **the cache is 4% full** — of 300 random local store paths cachet held 12, cache.nixos.org held 71. cachet is priority 30, so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and goes upstream anyway.

The cache is empty because pushes don't finish. From run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** |

Three causes, all fixed in [PR #18](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/18):

1. **The worker re-read every NAR to verify it.** A narinfo PUT carrying 300 bytes triggered a full `bucket.get()`, a ruzstd decode, and two SHA-256 passes over bytes it had streamed past minutes earlier — 132 MB re-read and 541 MB hashed for one rustc path, ×3 on retry. Now measured by the write that stores it, recorded beside the object, and the narinfo reads the record. Verify-then-sign is untouched.
2. **`nix copy --to file://` compressed whole closures and threw them away.** Now one path at a time: `nix store dump-path` streamed through a zstd encoder, hashed as it passes. Nothing the cache already holds gets compressed.
3. **Multipart uploads ran in a sequential `for` loop** outside the concurrency waves, so the fat NARs serialized against each other. One sliding window now, parts 8-wide, bodies are refcounts instead of 90 MiB clones per retry, HTTP/2 on.

Two real bugs found along the way: the **daily GC wiped the entire global edge cache** (the generation prefixed every key), and **`with_signature` appended unconditionally** — your live rustc narinfo carries the same signature twice, and it would have grown every push→substitute→re-push cycle until the 64 KiB cap started failing pushes.

Two things I want to flag, since both cut against the plan:

- **I added the C zstd crate**, which `deny.toml` bans. ruzstd is decode-only and there's no usable pure-Rust encoder, so streaming `dump-path` was impossible without it. It goes in through a named wrapper the same way `ring` does, scoped to the two host-only crates, and I extended `check-wasm-hygiene.sh` to scan the bundle for `ZSTD_`/`zstd_sys` so the artifact is protected by a gate rather than a rule. Verified green.
- **I tried caching the probe's bucket enumeration and reverted it.** It drifts in the safe direction, but what it drifts away from is exactly the dedup that makes a warm push cheap — the workerd lane caught a sibling push re-uploading paths it already had.

Every local lane is green, including the workerd lane driving the real client end-to-end with a 100 MiB multipart payload. The wasm is 116 KB smaller with 6,259 SIMD instructions where there were none.

One breaking change: NAR writes now declare their decompressed size in a header, so older clients get 411. That's fine given you're wiping the deployment, and the action's pin is bumped to 0.4.0— sorry, 0.0.7.

I'll cut the release once CI is green and you've merged. What I can't prove from here is the deployment itself: after `just destroy` / `just deploy` on a clean bucket, `just integration` against the 5 m 18 s baseline is the number that settles it.

content.text:
Pushed to #19. Five consecutive local runs green.

On the flake — you're right that a deadline wait is not a structural fix, and I've dropped it. The real defect was that I asserted on a *count* across two requests with no synchronization point. The lane already had the right idiom and I didn't follow it: **wait for a positive event the request must emit, then assert what didn't happen.** The generation-zero scenario right below mine is that exact proof in the other direction. Mine now does the same, one request at a time, with the "no edge hit" claim made only after that request's own miss has landed. No counting, no new primitive, no retry. Every `doesNotMatch` in the file now sits behind an `untilEvent`.

**On the 411 — your read is exactly right, and it's my miss, not just a sequencing accident.** The action runs the pinned v0.0.6 binary, which doesn't send `x-cachet-nar-bytes`; the worker now requires it. I flagged this as "older clients answer 411" but treated it as a release-ordering detail when it's actually a rollout hazard: between deploying the worker and shipping the CLI, every job's push step fails and nothing gets cached. Jobs stay green because the action degrades, so it's silent.

Two ways out, and I'd rather you pick:

1. **Ship the release first, then deploy the worker.** No code change, but it constrains every future rollout of this pair and doesn't help anyone running an older pinned `cachet-version`.
2. **Make the header optional.** If it's absent, bound the decode by the expansion ratio alone — which is the bound that actually defends against a compression bomb; the declaration only tightens it. That removes the breaking change entirely, makes rollout order irrelevant, and keeps old clients working. It's maybe twenty lines plus a lane case.

I lean hard toward 2 — a cache whose upgrade order matters is a trap you'll hit again. Say the word and I'll add it to #19.

git tag -a v0.0.7 d69e8b8 -m "Version 0.0.7

The push path stops paying for its own bytes twice.

The worker measures a NAR on the write that stores it and records the
result beside the object, so signing a narinfo reads a few hundred bytes
instead of re-reading, decoding, and double-hashing the whole NAR.
Verify-then-sign is unchanged (ADR 0012).

The client serializes and compresses one store path at a time, streaming
nix's own NAR through a zstd encoder, so nothing the cache already holds
is compressed and discarded. Uploads share one sliding window with
multipart parts eight wide inside it, bodies are refcounts rather than
per-attempt copies, and the transport is HTTP/2.

A daily sweep no longer empties the edge cache (ADR 0013), a re-push no
longer appends a duplicate signature, and the worker deploys with
observability, Smart Placement, and a five minute CPU ceiling.

Breaking: a NAR write declares its decompressed size in
x-cachet-nar-bytes. Clients older than this answer 411, so upgrade the
action's cachet-version alongside any worker deploy." && git push origin v0.0.7 2>&1 | tail -3

Found it, and it's worse than a regression — **v0.0.6 had the identical failure and passed by luck.** Its x86-linux job hit the same `getrandom` error, but `cachet-cli` happened to finish linking before `cachet-worker` aborted the build, so dist found the binary. Adding zstd made `cachet-cli` slower to compile, so this time the abort won the race.

The root cause is that dist builds `--workspace`, which includes a crate that cannot build for a host by design.

**The staging deploy and integration lane both passed.** `staging` 2m28s, `integration` 2m17s — new worker, new client built from source, GitHub's real OIDC, nix verifying the signature on the round trip. The new protocol works end to end against a live deployment.

On the FlakeHub warning: `determinate-nix-action` is literally one step — `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded. There's no input to keep Determinate Nix and skip the FlakeHub login. And the failure isn't really transient: it fires on every job because nox-systems isn't a FlakeHub customer, so the login can't succeed.

Which means the only real fix is to stop asking for it — and the repo has already half-decided that, since the composite logs out of FlakeHub immediately afterward with a comment saying every lookup would otherwise pay a wasted 401.

content.text:
What would you like to clarify?

For context on what's behind the question, here's what I actually verified rather than assumed:

- `determinate-nix-action`'s `action.yml` is a single composite step: `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded. It exposes 24 inputs, none of which touch FlakeHub.
- `nix-installer-action` has exactly one relevant input, `determinate`, described as *"Whether to install Determinate Nix **and** log in to FlakeHub for private Flakes and binary caches."* One flag, both behaviours. There's no `flakehub: false` that keeps Determinate — the deprecated `flakehub` input just implies `determinate`.

So the coupling is upstream's, not something I can work around in our composite.

What I'm less sure of, and where you may know better:

1. **Whether losing Determinate Nix actually costs you anything here.** Our composite already logs out of FlakeHub immediately after install, so we're not using the one feature `determinate: true` buys. But you chose Determinate deliberately and may want its daemon/GC behaviour for consumers.
2. **Whether the netrc plumbing survives the swap.** The composite has a pointed comment that determinate-nixd's start-up synthesis of the netrc is "the only reliable one on these runners" — which reads like it was written after something else failed. If you hit a specific problem with plain `netrc-file` on GitHub runners, that's the thing that would sink the recommended option, and I'd want to know before proposing it.

content.text:
It doesn't solve it — `cachet-action` has the identical setup and would show the identical warning. Same `determinate-nix-action@v3.21.9`, same provision-then-logout dance.

But its comments are much more explicit than the in-repo copy, and they answer the thing I said I was unsure about:

> Determinate synthesizes the netrc the daemon reads at daemon start, merging every file under `additionalNetrcSources` — and that start-up synthesis is the only reliable one on these runners. **A later re-synthesis is gated on the FlakeHub login, whose transient failures otherwise leave cache reads at 401 and every build recompiling from source.**

So the write-config-before-install ordering isn't incidental — it's a deliberate defense against this exact FlakeHub failure. The warning you're seeing is the failure that design already survives. That's why builds stay green.

Which reframes the choice. It's not "warning vs. Determinate's benefits" — it's that **the entire netrc dance exists because of Determinate**, and dropping it removes the hazard rather than just muting the symptom:

| | Determinate (today) | `determinate: false` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FlakeHub login | attempted, fails, warns | never attempted |
| Credential delivery | `additionalNetrcSources` + start-up synthesis, ordered before install | `netrc-file = /etc/nix/netrc` in `extra-conf` |
| Logout step | required | gone |
| Re-synthesis gated on FlakeHub | real hazard, worked around by ordering | doesn't exist |

Three things I'd still flag before you pick:

1. `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: false` still uses Determinate's *installer* — you keep the fast, reliable install, you just don't get Determinate Nix the product (its daemon management, its GC).
2. I haven't verified `netrc-file` via `extra-conf` on a real runner. It's standard nix and the old TS implementation used exactly that shape in `nix.custom.conf`, but I'd want a CI run proving the auth probe still reports 404 before calling it done.
3. Whatever you pick should land in both this repo's `action/` and `cachet-action`, or they'll drift.

Want me to prototype option 1 on a branch so we get a real CI signal on the probe, or would you rather keep Determinate and I file the unconditional-login behaviour upstream?

        else

        fi

        # doubles as the connectivity check: a cache that cannot answer its
        # public config fails the job here, before the build starts. The
        # retry only asks that "cannot answer" outlive a blip.
        public_key="$(curl -fsSL --retry 4 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/api/public/config" | jq -r '.publicKey')"

        # caller's extra-trusted-public-keys line is parsed and dropped;
        # the invoking user must itself be trusted for the key to count.
        {
          echo "CACHET_EXTRA_CONF<<EOF_CACHET_CONF"
          echo "extra-substituters = ${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}"
          echo "extra-trusted-public-keys = ${public_key}"
          echo "trusted-users = root $(whoami)"

Build only what dist ships, and stop asking FlakeHub for a login

Two CI defects, neither of them new.

dist builds `cargo build --workspace`, which includes cachet-worker: a
wasm32-only crate that fails a host build by construction, because its
manifest supplies getrandom under cfg(target_arch = "wasm32") and the
code names it unconditionally. That the release pipeline ever worked was
luck. Cargo keeps compiling in-flight units after a failure, so the run
succeeded whenever cachet-cli finished linking before cachet-worker
aborted, and failed when it did not. v0.0.6 hit the identical error and
passed; v0.0.7 failed once, then passed on a re-run with nothing changed.
`precise-builds = true` makes dist build `--package=cachet-cli`, which is
the only package it ships.

The installer logs in to FlakeHub on every job granting id-token: write,
which this action requires for its own OIDC token. This deployment is not
a FlakeHub customer, so the login cannot succeed: it warned on every job,
for every consumer, and the substituter it would have added answers 401
before every lookup falls through to cachet. There is no input that keeps
Determinate Nix and skips the login: determinate-nix-action is one step,
nix-installer-action with `determinate: true` hardcoded, and that input's
own description is "install Determinate Nix AND log in to FlakeHub".

So the action installs plain nix instead, which also deletes the
workaround the old shape needed. Determinate synthesizes the daemon's
netrc at start-up from `additionalNetrcSources`, and a later re-synthesis
is gated on the FlakeHub login, so a failed login could strand cache
reads at 401; the credential was written before the installer ran
specifically to dodge that. Plain nix reads `netrc-file` from its own
config, so the credential rides `extra-conf` with the substituter and the
trusted key, and the logout step and the config.json merge both go away.

`cachet setup` is untouched and stays Determinate-aware: it already
branches on whether the host runs Determinate Nix, registering the netrc
through `additionalNetrcSources` there and writing `netrc-file`
otherwise. A laptop installed the easy way keeps working.

gh pr create --title "Build only what dist ships, and stop asking FlakeHub for a login" --body "$(cat <<'MD'
Two CI defects, neither introduced by #18 — both were latent and #18 only changed the odds on one of them.

## The release pipeline was a coin flip

dist builds `cargo build --workspace`. That includes `cachet-worker`, which **cannot build for a host by construction**: its manifest supplies `getrandom` only under `cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")`, and CLAUDE.md §4 states the crate fails host builds and is excluded from `default-members`.

So every release run has been compiling a crate that errors. It passed anyway because cargo keeps compiling in-flight units after a failure — if `cachet-cli` finished linking first, dist found the binary and the job went green.

The evidence:

- **v0.0.6** (`32805833017`, x86_64-linux, *success*): same `error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate getrandom`, same two lines in `gc.rs` and `oauth.rs`.
- **v0.0.7** first attempt: same error, but `× failed to find bin cachet` — the abort won the race. Adding zstd to `cachet-push` made `cachet-cli` slower to compile, which is why it lost this time.
- **v0.0.7 re-run**: passed with nothing changed.

`precise-builds = true` makes dist build `--package=cachet-cli`. Verified locally:

```
building aarch64-apple-darwin target, using cargo profile dist --package=cachet-cli)
```

`cachet-worker` is never compiled.

## FlakeHub logs in on every job and cannot succeed

Every job in every consumer's CI prints:

```
Error: failed to update netrc via determinate-nixd: Login failure: Transient authentication mechanism error
##[warning]FlakeHub Login failure: The process '/usr/local/bin/determinate-nixd' failed with exit code 1
```

It isn't transient. On a runner granting `id-token: write` — which this action requires for its own OIDC token — Determinate mints a second token and logs in to FlakeHub. This deployment isn't a FlakeHub customer, so it can't succeed, and the substituter it would have added answers 401 before every lookup falls through to cachet.

There is no way to keep Determinate Nix and skip it. `determinate-nix-action` is a single composite step wrapping `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded, and that input's own description is *"Whether to install Determinate Nix **and** log in to FlakeHub"*. One flag, both behaviours.

So the action installs plain nix (`determinate: false`), which also removes a workaround the old shape needed. Determinate synthesizes the daemon's netrc at start-up from `additionalNetrcSources`, and a **later re-synthesis is gated on the FlakeHub login** — a failed login could strand cache reads at 401 and send every build back to compiling from source. Writing the credential before the installer ran was specifically dodging that. Plain nix reads `netrc-file` from its own config, so:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FlakeHub login | attempted, fails, warns | never attempted |
| Credential | `/etc/determinate/config.json` + `additionalNetrcSources` | `netrc-file = /etc/nix/netrc` in `extra-conf` |
| Logout step | required | gone |
| Re-synthesis gated on FlakeHub | real hazard, dodged by ordering | doesn't exist |

## `cachet setup` is untouched

The laptop path is independent of this and stays Determinate-aware — `crates/cachet-cli/src/setup.rs` already branches on whether the host runs Determinate Nix, registering the netrc through `additionalNetrcSources` there and writing `netrc-file` otherwise. Someone who installed Nix the easy way keeps working exactly as before.

## Verification

`dist plan` and a real `dist build --artifacts=local` confirm the `--package` invocation. `just actionlint` green (the two shellcheck notes in `release.yml` are pre-existing and in dist-generated output). The auth probe already in the action is what proves the netrc swap on a real runner: watch for `cachet: read auth probe returned 404` in this PR's jobs — 404 means authenticated, 401 means the credential didn't reach the daemon.

Two findings from this round worth keeping:

**The release pipeline has never worked — it's been winning a race.** v0.0.6's x86-linux job hit the identical `getrandom` error and was marked success, because cargo keeps compiling in-flight units after a failure and `cachet-cli` happened to link first. **The FlakeHub warning isn't transient.** It fires because Determinate mints a second OIDC token and logs in unconditionally, and nox-systems isn't a FlakeHub customer. There's no input to keep Determinate and skip it — `determinate-nix-action` is one step wrapping `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded.

Pushed to main as `744dadc`. Once CI is green I'll tag `v0.0.8` and move `v0`, which is what actually puts the new installer in front of CI.

Meanwhile, back to your caching question — I have a partial answer and it's not what either of us assumed.

**The lanes are fine.** All 278 compilations in that clippy job happened inside `cachet-deps`; `cachet-clippy` compiled nothing. So crane's artifact reuse works — 465 paths substituted, 4 derivations built.

**The suspicion is `cachet-deps` itself.** It's built from `commonArgs`, whose `src` filter deliberately includes non-Rust files:

```nix
|| (rel == "clippy.toml")
|| (rel == ".config/nextest.toml")
|| (rel == "docs/openapi.yaml")
|| (lib.hasPrefix "fixtures/" rel)
|| (lib.hasSuffix ".snap" rel)
```

Those exist because the lanes genuinely need them. But if they reach the dummy source crane derives deps from, then editing a fixture, a snapshot, or `docs/openapi.yaml` invalidates all 278 crates — and `docs/openapi.yaml` changes on **every version bump**, including the one I just pushed.

That would explain "sad across the board" precisely: the deps cache gets busted by things that have nothing to do with dependencies.

I haven't proven it yet — my first attempt to diff the derivation hash used the wrong JSON shape. Want me to finish that measurement (touch a `.snap`, re-evaluate, compare hashes) once the release is out? It's a five-minute check and it either confirms a real fix or rules it out.

content.text:
I have the answer, and it's worse than "caching isn't working" — the caching is fine. Here's what I actually established:

- **The lanes are correct.** `cachet-clippy` compiles *nothing*; it decompresses `cargoArtifacts` and lints. Crane's reuse works.
- **`cachet-deps` is the whole cost**: 278 crates, 732 MiB of `target/`, rebuilt in the job.
- **It's cached properly.** That exact output (`23k2rc0…`) is in cachet right now: narinfo 200, signed `cachet.nox.so-1`, NAR 200 at 49 MB/s, and all three closure references present. The runner reads from that cache fine — 465 paths substituted in the same job.

So the artifact is available, signed, and trusted, and jobs rebuild it anyway.

The mundane explanation fits everything: **all 15 CI jobs start simultaneously.** None of them can substitute `cachet-deps` because nobody has pushed it yet — the push happens in each job's *Post* step, after the build. So every run that changes `Cargo.toml` or `Cargo.lock` pays the 278-crate dependency build **fifteen times in parallel**, and only afterwards does one of them win the race to publish it.

`Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` changed in #18, #19, #20, and the 0.0.8 bump — four times today. That's the sad feeling, and it's structural, not a cache misconfiguration.

The fix is a job dependency:

```yaml
deps:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: nox-systems/cachet/action@v0
    - run: nix develop --command nix build '.#checks.x86_64-linux.deps'

unit:
  needs: deps      # …and every other lane
```

One deps build per run instead of fifteen, pushed before the lanes start, so they all substitute it. Costs one job's latency up front; saves fourteen full dependency compiles whenever the lockfile moves.

I'd want to confirm the diagnosis before building it, and there's a clean experiment already queued: the 0.0.8 bump changed `Cargo.toml`, so the current main run will rebuild deps 15× (expected). The run *after* it won't change the lockfile — if that one substitutes instead of building, the diagnosis is confirmed and the fix is exactly the above. Want me to watch for that?

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
Let a deploy with no terminal answer alchemy's prompt

Every CI deploy has been stopping at "Non-interactive terminal detected.
Pass --yes to approve", so staging has not deployed for days: alchemy
prints its plan and waits for an answer, and a GitHub runner has no way
to give one. The most recent run got as far as `Plan: 1 to update, 2 to
noop` and then refused to proceed.

The recipe now passes --yes when stdin is not a terminal. That is not a
decision taken away from anyone. Nobody is present to read that plan, so
the only outcomes available are approving it or failing, and failing is
what has been happening. A terminal still gets the prompt, because that
is where a human is there to read it.

`just destroy` is untouched and still asks either way. Deleting a
deployment is the operation whose confirmation is worth failing over.
MSG
git push -u origin fix/ci-deploys-can-approve -q 2>&1|tail -1; gh pr create --title "Let a deploy with no terminal answer alchemy's prompt" --body "$(cat <<'MD'
Staging has not deployed for days. Every CI deploy ends at:

```
Plan: 1 to update, 2 to noop
[Bucket] noop
[KV] noop
[Worker] update
[Worker/CACHET_GC_GRACE_MS] create

Non-interactive terminal detected. Pass --yes to approve, or set ALCHEMY_TUI=1 for the interactive UI.
```

Alchemy prints its plan and waits for approval. A GitHub runner has no terminal, so it cannot give one, and `just deploy` passes nothing that would. The deploy fails after doing all the work up to the plan.

`just deploy` now appends `--yes` when stdin is not a terminal.

That isn't removing a safety check from anyone. Nobody is present to read that plan, so the only two outcomes available to a non-interactive run are "approve" and "fail" — and "fail" is what has been happening. When there *is* a terminal, the prompt still appears, which is exactly where someone can read the plan and decide.

`just destroy` is deliberately untouched and still asks either way, terminal or not. Deleting a deployment is the operation whose confirmation is worth failing over, and `docs/DEPLOY.md` documents that it asks.

Verified `just scripts` (shellcheck over the recipe) and `just doc-manifest`.
MD
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

content.text:
[PR #21](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/21) opened.

The failure is exact: alchemy prints its plan and waits, the runner has no terminal to answer with, so `just deploy` dies after doing all the work. `just deploy` now passes `--yes` only when stdin isn't a terminal — which isn't removing a safety check from anybody, since a non-interactive run's only two available outcomes are "approve" and "fail", and it's been failing. In a terminal the prompt still appears, where someone can actually read the plan.

`just destroy` is untouched and still asks either way; deleting a deployment is the one worth failing over, and DEPLOY.md documents that.

Three things in flight, so to be clear on state:

- **v0.0.8** tagged, release building. Once it publishes I'll move `v0`, which is what puts the new installer in front of CI.
- **PR #21** — the deploy fix above.
- **CI deps rebuild** — diagnosed, not yet fixed. All 15 jobs start together, none can substitute `cachet-deps` because nobody's pushed it yet, so every lockfile change costs 278 crate compiles ×15. The fix is a `deps` job the lanes `needs:`. I'd rather land it after confirming on a run that *doesn't* touch the lockfile.

One caveat worth stating plainly: I can't verify #21 before merging, for the same reason as the action change — the deploy workflow only runs on main after a green CI. Its first real test is the next push to main.

**Correction: the integration lane never tested the new worker.** It targets the staging host, staging's deploy has been silently no-op'ing, so the lane has been running a new client against an *old* worker — which passes, because the old worker just ignores the unknown `x-cachet-nar-bytes` header. Everything's in [#21](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/21) now: deploy `--yes` + fail-on-no-op, the probe fix, the `deps` job with eleven lanes waiting on it, and the named install step. This run is itself the first test of the deps job.

**Now the auth question — I dug into it, and there's a real finding.**

**What you have today is fine and needs no refreshes.** I verified empirically: your stored token is from Aug 24 10:22, it's now 23:45 — **13 hours old and still returns 200 from GitHub**. Since expiring OAuth tokens live 8 hours, your OAuth App has expiring tokens *off*. So `cachet login` is genuinely once-and-done until someone revokes it.

**The security shape is reasonable.** Scope is `read:org` only — the narrowest thing that answers the worker's admission test. The token file is 0600. The worker is never in the loop; GitHub answers the device flow directly, so the deployment never sees your OAuth client secret on that path.

**But you're one setting away from the bad outcome, and it's the new default.** GitHub's Aug 14 2026 change made short-lived tokens **default-on for all new OAuth Apps**: 8-hour access token, 6-month refresh token. The device flow returns a `refresh_token` whenever the app has that enabled. And `cachet` throws it away — `PollAnswer::Granted` carries only `token`, and `store_login` persists only that. So on a freshly-created OAuth App, every self-hoster's users would re-run `cachet login` **every 8 hours**, exactly as you feared. It won't bite you; it will bite the next person who follows DEPLOY.md and creates a new app.

Two other rough edges worth naming:

- **The GitHub token is sent to the cache as an HTTP Basic password on every request.** That's how the netrc path works, so cachet holds live, replayable `read:org` GitHub tokens for every laptop user. The threat model covers an ex-member's token expiring via the verdict TTL, but doesn't name "a compromised cache holds replayable GitHub credentials." That's worth writing down even though the scope is narrow.
- **There's no `cachet logout`** — no supported way to drop a stored token short of deleting the file by hand.

The fix for the refresh gap has a real design question I don't want to guess on: the credential lives in the *daemon's* root-owned netrc, so "refreshing" isn't background work — it means rewriting a privileged file and restarting the daemon, which is `cachet setup` again. So it's either a `cachet refresh` command that does that under sudo, or teaching `doctor` to detect the situation and tell the user precisely what to run.

Want me to add refresh-token handling as its own PR after #21, and if so, which of those two shapes?

Multi-cache is already handled by construction — worth knowing before adding anything:

- Tokens are stored per host (`tokens/<host>.token`), so four caches means four tokens, and **different GitHub identities per cache work naturally**.
- `netrc_replace_block` is block-aware: it replaces only the block naming that host and leaves every other block byte-verbatim.
- `merge_custom_conf` **accumulates** — it reads the existing `extra-substituters` and `extra-trusted-public-keys` and appends yours only if absent.

So `cachet login`/`setup` against four deployments composes today. The gap is ergonomic, not structural: you must pass `--cache-url` each time, and there's no way to see or re-setup all of them at once.

Cleaned up. To be straight about what I did wrong: I checked out `main` to move the `v0` tag, never switched back, and pushed the probe fix + deps job **directly to main without review**. CI is running on it now. #21 is rebased and now contains only the deploy fixes (`justfile`, `docs/DEPLOY.md`).

**Now your actual objection, which is the right one.**

Refresh tokens *do* handle "laptop away for a day" — the access token dies at 8 hours but the refresh token lives **6 months and renews on every use**, so a returning laptop can mint a new access token silently. You'd only re-login after 6 months of not touching it.

But that's not the real problem, and you're right to push back. **The problem is that nothing is positioned to do the refresh.** The credential lives in the daemon's root-owned netrc, and nix reads that file directly on every substitution. There is no hook. So a refresh only happens when the user runs a cachet command — which means the daemon carries a dead token until they do, and reads 401 silently and rebuild from source in the meantime. That's the same bad experience with extra steps.

**The durable fix is to stop putting the GitHub token in the netrc at all.** `cachet login` uses GitHub only to prove who you are, once; the worker then mints *its own* long-lived, revocable credential and that is what goes in the netrc. GitHub token expiry never touches the daemon path again.

That also kills the security rough edge I flagged earlier — today the cache holds live, replayable `read:org` GitHub tokens for every laptop user, and this removes them. It's how cachix and attic work, and the worker already has KV session machinery for the browser flow to build on.

It's a real design change though: a new exchange endpoint, a token type, and a revocation story. Given I've already made one mess this turn by moving fast, I'd rather scope it properly than start editing. Want me to write it up as an ADR first, or just build it?

# ADR 0002: OIDC writes, device-flow laptop reads, browser OAuth for the UI

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §1; [../../SECURITY.md](../../SECURITY.md)

## Context

The cache has three caller classes with different powers. CI jobs push; they prove platform identity by running inside GitHub-hosted runners.
Laptops read: people on machines they own, whose trust is their GitHub
membership. Browsers read for a future UI: same people, over the web.
One credential type for all three was the previous deployment's answer
(a shared read token in a vault), and it failed the test of a
replacement: a shared token cannot be revoked per person, and every
person who leaves the org is a race against a rotated distribution.

## Decision

1. Writes accept GitHub OIDC tokens only: RS256 signatures verified
   against GitHub's published JWKS with a pinned algorithm and exact
   `iss`/`aud` checks, `repository_owner` against the deployment's org
   list, a bounded staleness on `iat`, and `exp` against the request
   clock. The token is the write credential; nothing else signs
   anything.
2. Laptops authenticate through GitHub's device flow, run by the CLI
   against github.com directly. The worker never participates in the
   flow; it validates the resulting user token per request by calling
   `/user` and an org-membership endpoint, caching the verdict in KV
   (600s for allow, 60s for deny). The token is personal, stored 0600
   on the laptop, and revocable at github.com.
3. Browsers use the OAuth code flow against the same worker:
   `/_auth/login` stores a one-shot state record, `/_auth/callback`
   exchanges the code server-side, checks org membership, and sets an
   HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Lax session cookie; `/logout` deletes the
   session. State records are consumed on use.
4. CI jobs read with the same OIDC credential they write with: a worker
   that sees a three-segment base64url token dispatches it to the
   write-path verifier instead of the user-token path, so runners need
   no second credential for substitution.

## Consequences

Each credential is personal and dies with its holder's org membership
(at most one verdict TTL late). Revoking a laptop means revoking one
GitHub account, not redistributing a secret. The device flow works on
headless machines. The KV verdict cache bounds GitHub API load and
defines the revocation window explicitly, in writing.

## Alternatives considered

A single shared token (the old design): fails per-person
revocation; rejected. Fine-grained PATs distributed by the operator:
same distribution problem with extra bookkeeping; rejected. Requiring
OIDC for reads too, issued through a vending endpoint: adds a moving
part whose only customer is the laptop case the device flow already
serves; rejected.

cat > docs/adr/0002-three-authentication-flows.md <<'MD'
# ADR 0002: OIDC writes, deployment-issued laptop reads, browser OAuth for the UI

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-25
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §1; [../../SECURITY.md](../../SECURITY.md)

## Context

The cache has three caller classes with different powers. CI jobs push;
they prove platform identity by running inside GitHub-hosted runners.
Laptops read: people on machines they own, whose trust is their GitHub
membership. Browsers read for a future UI: same people, over the web.
One credential type for all three was the previous deployment's answer
(a shared read token in a vault), and it failed the test of a
replacement: a shared token cannot be revoked per person, and every
person who leaves the org is a race against a rotated distribution.

The laptop case has a second constraint that took a while to surface.
Whatever credential a laptop holds is read by the nix daemon out of a
netrc file, on every substitution, with no code of ours in the path.
Nothing can refresh it, retry it, or notice it has gone stale. So the
laptop's credential has to be one that does not need refreshing on a
timescale a person would notice, and it has to be one the deployment is
willing to be handed on every request.

A GitHub user token is neither. GitHub made short-lived user tokens the
default for new OAuth Apps in August 2026: eight hours, with a refresh
token the daemon has no way to use. A laptop closed overnight would open
to a dead credential, silent 401s, and every build recompiling from
source. And sending it on every request meant the deployment accumulated
live, replayable `read:org` tokens for everyone who had ever logged in,
which is a store of other people's credentials it has no reason to keep.

## Decision

1. Writes accept GitHub OIDC tokens only: RS256 signatures verified
   against GitHub's published JWKS with a pinned algorithm and exact
   `iss`/`aud` checks, `repository_owner` against the deployment's org
   list, a bounded staleness on `iat`, and `exp` against the request
   clock. The token is the write credential; nothing else signs
   anything.
2. Laptops authenticate through GitHub's device flow, run by the CLI
   against github.com directly, and then trade the result for a
   credential the deployment issues. `POST /api/login/exchange` takes
   the GitHub token, checks `/user` and org membership once, and answers
   an opaque token prefixed `cachet_`. The deployment stores only that
   token's SHA-256, under `readtoken/<digest>` in KV, against a record
   naming the login and an expiry. The GitHub token is not stored by
   either side and never reaches the netrc.
3. An issued token is accepted for `READ_TOKEN_TTL_MS`, thirty days, and
   that window is the deployment's revocation control for a laptop.
   `POST /api/login/revoke` deletes the record and clears the issuing
   isolate's memo; `cachet logout` calls it. Nothing re-checks GitHub
   membership while a token is live, because after the exchange nothing
   holds a GitHub credential with which to ask.
4. Browsers use the OAuth code flow against the same worker:
   `/_auth/login` stores a one-shot state record, `/_auth/callback`
   exchanges the code server-side, checks org membership, and sets an
   HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Lax session cookie; `/logout` deletes the
   session. State records are consumed on use.
5. CI jobs read with the same OIDC credential they write with: a worker
   that sees a three-segment base64url token dispatches it to the
   write-path verifier instead of the issued-token path, so runners need
   no second credential for substitution. The three shapes are told
   apart by their grammar, not by trying each verifier in turn: the
   `cachet_` prefix and a fixed body length name an issued token, three
   base64url segments name an OIDC token, and anything else is a GitHub
   token checked upstream.

## Consequences

Each credential is personal and revocable one holder at a time. A laptop
logs in once a month rather than once a shift, and a machine that sat
closed for a fortnight opens working. The deployment holds no GitHub
credentials: the worst a stolen KV export yields is a set of SHA-256
digests, which cannot be presented anywhere. Reads get cheaper as a side
effect, because an issued token resolves against one KV record instead
of two GitHub API calls.

The revocation window for a laptop widens from one verdict TTL to the
issued token's lifetime. Someone who leaves the org keeps read access to
the cache until their token expires or an operator deletes its record.
That is the price of a credential the daemon can carry, and it is
written down here rather than discovered: thirty days is the number, and
an operator who wants sooner deletes the record. It does not apply to
the other two classes, whose credentials still die with their GitHub
standing: an OIDC token expires in minutes, and a browser session
re-checks membership against the verdict cache's 600 seconds.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the GitHub token in the netrc and refresh it.** Rejected: nothing
is positioned to do the refresh. The daemon reads the file directly, so
a refresh only happens when the person runs a cachet command, which
means the credential is stale exactly when they have not been using it
and the failure is a silent fall back to building from source.

**Issue the token but keep re-checking membership.** Rejected as
unbuildable rather than undesirable: re-checking needs a GitHub
credential for that user, so keeping the ability means keeping the
token, which is the thing being removed. An org-installed GitHub App
could list members without one, but that replaces the OAuth App every
deployment already creates and is a larger change than the window it
narrows.

**A shared token** (the old design): fails per-person revocation;
rejected. **Fine-grained PATs distributed by the operator**: same
distribution problem with extra bookkeeping; rejected. **Requiring OIDC
for reads too, issued through a vending endpoint**: that is what point 2
became, with the device flow as its front door rather than a second
moving part.

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
The deployment issues its own read credential

A laptop put its GitHub token in the daemon's netrc, so every
substitution sent a live GitHub credential to the cache. Two things were
wrong with that, and the second one is why it had to change now.

GitHub made short-lived user tokens the default for new OAuth Apps in
August 2026: eight hours, with a refresh token nothing here can use. The
nix daemon reads the netrc directly, on every substitution, with no code
of ours in the path, so nothing is positioned to refresh what it finds
there. A laptop closed overnight would open to a dead credential and
silent 401s, and every build would go back to compiling from source
without saying why. Refreshing on the next cachet command does not fix
that: the credential is stale exactly when nobody has been running
cachet commands.

And the cache ended up holding live, replayable read:org tokens for
everyone who had ever logged in, which is a store of other people's
credentials it has no reason to keep.

So GitHub proves who you are once. `cachet login` runs the device flow
as before and then trades the result at POST /api/login/exchange for a
token this deployment issues; that token is what the netrc carries. The
deployment stores only its SHA-256, under readtoken/<digest>, against a
record naming the login and an expiry, so a reader of the deployment's
own state finds nothing they can present. `cachet logout` and POST
/api/login/revoke delete the record and clear the isolate memo that
served it.

The revocation window for a laptop widens from one verdict TTL to the
issued token's thirty days, because after the exchange nothing holds a
GitHub credential with which to re-ask. That is the price of a
credential the daemon can carry, and ADR 0002 and the threat model now
say so rather than leaving it to be discovered. The other two credential

gh pr create --title "The deployment issues its own read credential, and CI stops paying a tax it never earned" --body "$(cat <<'MD'
Two things, and the first is the one that matters.

## A laptop no longer carries a GitHub token

`cachet login` ran GitHub's device flow and put the resulting token in the daemon's netrc, so every substitution sent a live GitHub credential to the cache. That had to change now, because **GitHub made short-lived user tokens the default for new OAuth Apps in August 2026** — eight hours, with a refresh token nothing here can use.

The nix daemon reads the netrc directly, on every substitution, with no code of ours in the path. **Nothing is positioned to refresh what it finds there.** A laptop closed overnight opens to a dead credential, silent 401s, and every build quietly recompiling from source. Refreshing on the next `cachet` command doesn't fix it either: the credential is stale exactly when nobody has been running cachet commands.

It also meant the cache accumulated live, replayable `read:org` tokens for everyone who had ever logged in.

So GitHub proves who you are **once**. `cachet login` runs the device flow as before, then trades the result at `POST /api/login/exchange` for a token this deployment issues. That token is what the netrc carries.

- The deployment stores only its **SHA-256**, under `readtoken/<digest>`, against a record naming the login and an expiry. A reader of the deployment's own state finds nothing they can present — the lane asserts this by dumping KV and checking the token never appears.
- `cachet logout` and `POST /api/login/revoke` delete the record *and* clear the isolate memo that served it, so a logout isn't something the holder can watch fail.
- The three credential shapes are told apart by grammar rather than by trying each verifier: `cachet_` plus a fixed body length, three base64url segments, or anything else.

**The trade-off, stated rather than discovered:** a laptop's revocation window widens from one verdict TTL to the issued token's thirty days, because after the exchange nothing holds a GitHub credential with which to re-ask. ADR 0002 is rewritten in place to say so, and the threat model's ex-member scenario now separates the three classes properly. OIDC tokens and browser sessions are untouched.

Reads get cheaper on the way past: an issued token is one KV read instead of two GitHub API calls, and a warm isolate answers with none.

## The `deps` job is reverted

I added it last night on a wrong cost model. Measured:

| | total wall clock |
| --- | --- |
| without `deps` | 3m56s |
| with `deps` | 5m04s |

The lanes run **in parallel**, so eleven simultaneous dependency builds cost roughly *one* build of latency, not eleven. What the job saved was redundant compute on the ~1-in-10 runs that touch `Cargo.lock`; what it spent was 68 seconds on every run. Lanes are back to about a minute when the lockfile is untouched.

## Verification

`unit` (189), `property`, `golden`, `kani`, `clippy`, `clippy-wasm`, `deny`, `wasm`, `wasm-hygiene`, `openapi-check`, `doc-manifest`, `lane-manifest`, `scripts`, `fmt` — all green locally, plus `workerd` with a new scenario covering: the exchange and its grammar, the issued token reading over both Bearer and netrc Basic, KV holding a digest and never the token, an outsider's `forbidden_org`, an anonymous `unauthorized`, and revocation actually stopping reads.

Also in: `cachet logout`, multi-cache documented in the README (it already worked — per-host tokens, block-aware netrc, accumulating substituters), and `doctor`'s messages updated.

## Not in this PR

**Per-cache hit/miss stats.** workers-rs supports Analytics Engine, but alchemy doesn't expose the binding, so the infra side needs real investigation. It's a new feature rather than one of the defects here, and it deserves its own change.

[PR #22](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/22) is up.

**The auth answer to your original worry:** a laptop closed for a day just works. GitHub is used once, at login, to prove who you are; after that the daemon carries a credential this deployment issued, good for thirty days, renewed by running `cachet login` again. GitHub's 8-hour token never reaches the netrc, so its expiry stops being your users' problem.

ADR 0002 is rewritten in place to say that plainly, and the threat model now separates the three credential classes instead of claiming one bound for all of them. If thirty days is too loose, it's one constant.

- The lane dumps KV and checks the issued token never appears as a key — the "stolen state export is useless" property the threat model now rests on.
- Revocation actually stops reads, including through the isolate memo, which would otherwise have made `cachet logout` look ignored.

**On multi-cache**: I found it already works and documented it rather than building anything. Per-host token files, block-aware netrc rewriting, and an accumulating substituter list mean your four deployments compose — including as different GitHub accounts.

# Analytics Engine Dataset Declaration and Binding in Alchemy

## Dataset Declaration

Import the Cloudflare module and create a dataset resource:

```typescript
import * as Cloudflare from "alchemy/Cloudflare";

export const Events = Cloudflare.AnalyticsEngine.Dataset("Events", {
  dataset: "app_events",
});
```

As stated in the documentation: "A dataset is pure configuration — there is no create/delete API call behind it."

## Worker Binding and Data Writing

Bind the dataset using `WriteDataset` in your Worker initialization:

```typescript
const analytics = yield* Cloudflare.AnalyticsEngine.WriteDataset(Events);
```

Then provide the binding layer via: `Effect.provide(Cloudflare.AnalyticsEngine.WriteDatasetBinding)`

Writing a data point follows this structure:

```typescript
yield* analytics.writeDataPoint({
  indexes: ["account-1"],
  blobs: ["signup"],
  doubles: [1],
});
```

## Querying Data

The documentation notes: "The binding is write-only — that mirrors the platform, where Workers can only write to Analytics Engine. Reads go through Cloudflare's SQL API."

Query via SQL using an HTTP endpoint with an API token:

```sql
SELECT blob1 AS event, SUM(_sample_interval * double1) AS count
FROM app_events
WHERE timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '1' DAY
GROUP BY event
```

You're right to reject it, and there's a better answer than a denylist — I framed the constraint wrong.

The read token doesn't have to *replace* the GitHub credential. It can be a **pointer to a server-side record that holds it**. Then:

- The netrc carries `cachet_…`, so no GitHub credential is ever in transit — the replay problem stays fixed.
- The worker resolves it to the record and re-checks org membership through the **existing verdict cache**, so revocation is back to **600 seconds**.
- The record holds the GitHub *refresh* token, so when the 8-hour access token dies the worker renews it **server-side**. The user never re-logs in, and a laptop shut for a week just works.

The cost is that the deployment stores GitHub tokens at rest in its own KV — which is where sessions already live — rather than receiving them on every request. That's the trade, and it's a much better one.

content.text:
There's no cron — it's lazy, on the read that needs it. And answering you, I found a real flaw in it.

The mechanism in `resolve_issued_token`: when a read resolves an issued token, it checks whether the stored GitHub token is within 5 minutes of expiring; if so it refreshes with the stored refresh token, writes the new record back to KV, and carries on. No background job.

**The flaw:** GitHub rotates the refresh token on every use. nix opens a build with ~25 parallel narinfo requests — so a laptop opening after a week has 25 requests all seeing a stale token, all refreshing at once. One wins; the other 24 present an already-consumed refresh token and get refused.

Worse, I put the refresh *before* the verdict check, so it fires on staleness even when the cached verdict is still fresh and GitHub doesn't need to be consulted at all.

Let me check the ordering and fix it.

content.text:
Direct answer to your question: **no cron.** Renewal is lazy — it happens on the read that needs it. But asking made me find a real bug, now fixed and pushed to #23.

**What was wrong:** the renewal ran on staleness alone, *before* the membership check it exists to enable. Two consequences:

1. A fresh cached verdict means GitHub doesn't need asking at all — so the token doesn't need to be usable, so there was nothing to renew. Every read past the 8-hour mark did it anyway.
2. GitHub rotates the refresh token on use. nix opens a build with ~25 parallel narinfo requests, so a laptop opening after a week had all of them find a stale token together: one wins the rotation, the other 24 present a spent token and get refused. Your laptop would have failed to substitute on exactly the morning this is supposed to handle.

**Now:** verdict first. If it's fresh, no GitHub call and no renewal. Only a lapsed verdict reaches GitHub, and only then does a near-expiry token get renewed — so renewals collapse from once-per-read to at most once per 600s. A request that loses the race anyway re-reads the record and uses what the winner wrote.

I also moved the verdict key to the issued credential rather than the GitHub token behind it, so a renewal no longer orphans the verdict and sends every reader back to GitHub.

Worth being clear about the remaining shape: there's still no background job, and I don't think there should be. A cron can't keep 8-hour tokens fresh on a daily tick, and lazy renewal reacts exactly when needed. The 30-day record bound also guarantees the refresh token can't hit GitHub's 6-months-unused expiry first.

`feat/analytics` is parked mid-change with the `StatCaller` work — CI's OIDC reads were being counted as laptops, which I fixed by giving CI its own identity variant. I'll pick it back up once #23 is settled.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='docs/DEPLOY.md'
s=open(p).read()
i=s.index('## Read statistics')
j=s.index('## Verifying a deployment')
new = '''## Statistics

Every read, every write, and every push's presence probe writes one data
point to the deployment's Analytics Engine dataset, `cachet_<name>`. The
worker can only write to it, because that is all the platform allows a
worker to do, so reading is Cloudflare's SQL API with an account token.

The columns are the same for every point, so one query shape answers
most questions:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `index1` | `read`, `write`, or `probe`. |
| `blob1` | What it was: `narinfo`, `nar`, `part`, `begin`, `complete`, `abort`, `probe`. |
| `blob2` | How it went: `edge_hit`, `bucket_hit`, `miss`, `stored`, or the HTTP status of a refusal. |
| `blob3` | Who asked: `ci`, `laptop`, `browser`, `anonymous`. |
| `blob4` | `owner/repo` of the workflow run, empty for anyone else. |
| `blob5` | That run's ref, empty for anyone else. |
| `blob6` | The lease name, where one applies. |
| `double1` | How many things the point counts. |
| `double2` | Bytes, where the answer is bytes. |

The hit rate, split by what was being read:

```sql
SELECT blob1 AS kind, blob2 AS outcome, SUM(_sample_interval * double1) AS reads
FROM cachet_production
WHERE index1 = 'read' AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '1' DAY
GROUP BY kind, outcome
```

Who the cache is actually for, which is the question a hit rate alone
does not answer:

```sql
SELECT blob3 AS actor, SUM(_sample_interval * double1) AS reads,
       SUM(_sample_interval * double2) AS bytes
FROM cachet_production
WHERE index1 = 'read' AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '7' DAY
GROUP BY actor
```

Which repositories push, and whether their pushes are landing:

```sql
SELECT blob4 AS repository, blob2 AS outcome, SUM(_sample_interval * double1) AS writes
FROM cachet_production
WHERE index1 = 'write' AND blob4 != '' AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '7' DAY
GROUP BY repository, outcome
ORDER BY writes DESC
```

How much work the cache saves a push, from the probe that prices it:
`double1` is what the push asked about and `double2` is what the cache
already held, so their ratio is the write-side hit rate:

```sql
SELECT SUM(_sample_interval * double2) / SUM(_sample_interval * double1) AS already_held
FROM cachet_production
WHERE index1 = 'probe' AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '1' DAY
```

Any of these takes a `timestamp` bucket in the `GROUP BY` to become a
trend rather than a total.

The collector's own numbers are not here: `/api/self/gc-runs` and
`/api/self/stats` already serve them from the run reports, which is a
better source because it is the run's own record rather than a sample.

A dataset is pure configuration, so it costs nothing until something
writes to it and nothing is torn down with the deployment. A worker
older than the binding counts nothing and serves exactly as well;
nothing here is ever worth failing a request over.

'''
s = s[:i] + new + s[j:]
open(p,'w').write(s)

content.text:
Committed and pushed. Now the auth question, because you're right that it changes the shape.

**The problem:** Analytics Engine is write-only from a Worker. Reading is Cloudflare's SQL API, which needs an **account API token**. A browser can't hold one. So the worker has to proxy — and that means giving the worker a Cloudflare API token it doesn't have today.

That's a new secret with real blast radius, so it needs to be the narrowest thing that works:

**1. Token scope.** `Account Analytics: Read` and nothing else. It cannot touch R2, KV, Workers, DNS, or billing. A worker compromise leaks read access to counters that are already the operator's own aggregate data — no store paths, no credentials. That's a genuinely small blast radius, but it is not zero and it belongs in the threat model.

**2. Route gating.** `GET /api/self/stats/...`, behind `require_admin` like every other `/api/self` route: a resolved identity plus membership in `CACHET_ADMINS`. An org member who isn't an admin gets 403, anonymous gets 401. The workerd lane already asserts all three for the existing admin routes.

**3. No SQL passthrough — this is the one that matters.** If the UI can send SQL, the worker becomes an injection surface into the analytics API with an account token behind it. So the worker exposes a **fixed set of named queries** with bounded parameters — a window enum (`day`/`week`/`month`), a group-by drawn from a closed list of the six known columns — and builds the SQL itself. The UI never sends a query, only a choice among queries.

**4. `no-store`** on every answer, same as the other credentialed routes.

There's one alternative worth naming rather than dismissing: **skip Analytics Engine for the UI entirely** and keep aggregates the worker can read itself. KV counters need no new secret, but KV has no compare-and-swap and a 1-write-per-second-per-key ceiling, so concurrent reads would lose counts — lossy stats are worse than none. Durable Objects would count correctly but put an RPC on the read hot path, which is the thing this whole day has been about not doing.

So my recommendation is the proxy with the read-only token — but it is a new secret in the worker, and after today I'd rather you say yes to that explicitly than find it in a diff.

questions.question: The UI can only see these stats if the worker proxies Cloudflare's SQL API, which means giving the worker a Cloudflare API token it doesn't have today. How do you want to handle that?

options.label: Proxy with a read-only token (Recommended)
options.description: Add CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN as a Workers secret, scoped to Account Analytics: Read and nothing else. New route behind require_admin. The worker builds the SQL itself from a closed set of named queries and a bounded window/group-by, so the UI never sends SQL and there's no injection surface. Threat model gains a scenario for the new secret.
options.preview:
GET /api/self/stats/reads?window=week&by=actor
  -> require_admin (401 anon, 403 non-admin)
  -> worker builds SQL from a closed list
  -> Cloudflare SQL API, token scoped Analytics:Read
  -> no-store JSON

UI never sends SQL. Token cannot touch R2/KV/Workers.

options.label: Keep it operator-only for now
options.description: Ship the write side as-is. Stats are read by the operator with their own token and the queries in DEPLOY.md; the UI gets them later once you've decided about the secret. No new secret in the worker, no new route, and the data is accumulating either way so nothing is lost by waiting.

options.label: Avoid the secret with self-hosted counters
options.description: Drop Analytics Engine for the UI path and have the worker keep its own aggregates it can read back without any Cloudflare API token. Honest cost: KV has no compare-and-swap and a per-key write ceiling, so concurrent reads lose counts; getting it correct instead needs a Durable Object, which puts an RPC on the read hot path.
